passage:
Kavitha's first week in Pune felt like a film montage: a rooftop lunch with her new team, autos honking, a river walk at sunset, and a phone full of photos to send to Amma. She barely thought of Madurai. Every hour was packed with something new.

By week three the shine was scratched. The flat search ate her Sundays, Bhupen the broker never picked up, and the landlord wanted a document she did not have. The canteen's sambar tasted wrong. The auto drivers answered in a language she only half followed. "At home this takes ten minutes," she muttered, for the fifth time that week.

In the sixth week, on a Sunday evening, her flatmate Zubin was out and the flat was quiet. She stirred instant noodles and thought of her mother's rasam, the neighbours who knew her name, her bed with the old blue sheet. She cried into the sink, quietly, and wondered whether coming had been a mistake. She rang Amma and said only, "I'm just tired," heard the pressure cooker whistle in the background, and cried again.

qa.q: What did Kavitha think of while stirring noodles on the quiet Sunday?
qa.a: She thought of her mother's rasam, the neighbours who knew her name, and her bed with the old blue sheet.

qa.q: How did Kavitha's first week differ from her sixth, and what caused the change?
qa.a: In the first week every hour was packed with something new, so she barely thought of Madurai. By week three the flat search, the food and the language wore her down, and by the sixth week she was homesick and crying, which does not mean the move was wrong.

qa.q: What was Kavitha feeling when she cried into the sink?
qa.a: She felt homesick and like an outsider, and she wondered whether coming had been a mistake.

qa.q: What could Kavitha do to ease the homesickness?
qa.a: She could keep regular calls with Amma, cook familiar food, find people from her own region, and give the city more time.

grounding: Shows the first relocation stages: the excitement of arrival, small logistical frustrations comparing everything to home, and homesickness with culture shock.

passage:
The rank list left no room for doubt. Harsha scrolled to the bottom of the admit list at six in the morning and did not find his number. By breakfast the sentence in his head had hardened: I am stupid, and Papa's money is wasted. He thought of the coaching fees, the extra tiffin his mother packed, and the way the whole family had planned its year around this one exam. A single test had become a verdict on all of him.

He told Lokesh, who texted twice, that the paper had been set unfairly and the invigilator had rushed them. Then he stopped replying to Lokesh and told nobody else. On Sunday his father asked, "Anything on the result?" and Harsha said, "Not up yet."

That evening at his aunt's house the truth reached the room anyway, through a neighbour's son. Over tea an uncle counted off cousins' ranks and glanced at Harsha. "Some children just don't apply themselves." His cousin Gopika, visiting from Hyderabad, watched Harsha's face go blank. She followed him to the balcony that same hour. "One result isn't you," she said. "Do you want to sit with me and work out what comes next?" He nodded without looking up, and then, to his own surprise, wept.

qa.q: What did Harsha tell his father on Sunday about the result?
qa.a: He said it was not up yet.

qa.q: How did Harsha's shame and hiding lead to the moment on the balcony?
qa.a: Harsha turned one failed test into a verdict that he was stupid and his father's money was wasted, then blamed the paper and hid the result. When the truth reached his aunt's house and an uncle counted off cousins' ranks, Gopika saw his face go blank and offered a quiet word that one result is not the person.

qa.q: What was Harsha feeling when the uncle counted off the cousins' ranks?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and numb, and his face went blank.

qa.q: What could the family do to support Harsha now?
qa.a: They could stop comparing him with cousins, say that one result is not the person, and sit down with him to plan next steps.

grounding: Shows a teen's failure arc: shame turning one test into a verdict on the self, blaming and hiding, and a cousin offering a quiet word and a plan when the family compares.

passage:
Vinita felt Lalit slipping away in small ways: his replies came in the evening rather than the afternoon, and his hand was always on his phone. What she wanted was a proper talk, and what she felt underneath was fear of being left. It came out as hints. "Busy again?" and "Must be nice to have so many friends," in a tone sharper than she meant.

On Thursday she sent six messages before lunch. When Lalit walked into the canteen at three, she stood up. "What's happening to us? Are we okay? Tell me." Gautam, at the next bench, pretended to study his notes. Vinita believed that pressing harder would get her through to him.

Lalit felt the room tilt. What he heard was: you are failing, answer now. His ears rang. He picked up his bag, said "I need air," put in his earphones and walked toward the hostel gate. He thought he was avoiding a fight. Vinita, standing alone with her tray, felt as though she had been left in the middle of a sentence.

qa.q: How many messages did Vinita send before lunch on Thursday?
qa.a: She sent six messages.

qa.q: How did Vinita's pursuit and Lalit's withdrawal look from each of their sides?
qa.a: Vinita believed pressing harder would get her through to him, so she sent six messages and stood up in the canteen. Lalit heard criticism and demand, felt overwhelmed and left with his earphones thinking he was avoiding a fight, while she felt left in the middle of a sentence.

qa.q: What was Vinita feeling under her sharp hints?
qa.a: She felt fear of being left, along with a wish for a proper talk.

qa.q: What could Vinita do differently the next evening?
qa.a: She could say she misses him and ask for a quiet talk at a set time, instead of pressing him in the canteen.

grounding: Shows the start of a pursue-withdraw cycle: rising unmet need, the partner's pursuit, and the other's flooded withdrawal.

passage:
Rohan's silence at dinner proved what Sarita already feared, so that night she typed a very long message, then a longer one, and at midnight a voice note that shook. By morning her eyes were red and her tone was an accusation: "You don't care. You never talk to me." Rohan read the texts on the stairs and felt his chest close. He stayed out until late. The louder she pushed, the further he stepped back, and each was sure the other had started it.

On Sunday, in a calm hour at the park, Sarita said, "The more I push, the more you disappear, and the more you disappear, the more I push." Rohan stared at the grass, then laughed a little. "That's exactly it." For the first time it was the two of them against the loop, not each against the other.

They practised. "I miss you and I'm scared," Sarita said one evening, instead of "you never talk." Rohan said, "Give me twenty minutes and I'll be back," and put the kettle on. Twenty minutes later he was, holding two cups. She noticed that she had waited without counting the minutes.

qa.q: What did Rohan do twenty minutes after asking for time?
qa.a: He came back holding two cups.

qa.q: How did the loop work before they named it, and what changed once they did?
qa.a: The more Sarita pushed with long messages and accusations, the further Rohan stepped back, and each was sure the other had started it. Once they named the loop in a calm hour they were together against it, and she used a softer ask while he used a promised return.

qa.q: How was Rohan feeling when he read Sarita's morning texts on the stairs?
qa.a: He felt overwhelmed and pressured: his chest closed and he stayed out late.

qa.q: What could Sarita do if Rohan takes longer than the twenty minutes?
qa.a: She could gently remind him of what he promised and tell him she misses him, without accusing.

grounding: Shows the later pursue-withdraw stages: intensified pursuit, naming the pattern as the shared enemy, and a softer ask matched by reliable return.

passage:
For a year Shreya had kept a notebook with two columns: what she had been taught, and what she actually found true. She read the verses she had grown up reciting, then commentaries she had never opened. On Sunday walks she asked her cousin Ishita, a believer who liked hard questions, why prayer worked for her. "I don't know that it works," Ishita said. "I know it holds me." At lunch she asked Yusuf, a colleague who called himself a sceptic, what he did with grief. He answered honestly and then asked her the same. She let the questions stay open, without panic.

Over the next year the answer settled quietly. She no longer felt a creed. What she felt was a set of values she had kept: kindness, keeping promises, giving without an audience. She told nobody for a month, and then told Ishita first.

At Diwali she stood at the back of her family's puja, not reciting, and lit the lamps beside her grandmother because the light and the smell of ghee felt like home. She did not argue with her uncle's sermon and did not ask anyone to think as she did. Ishita passed her a sweet. "Same table," Ishita said.

qa.q: Who did Shreya tell first about where her seeking had led?
qa.a: She told Ishita first.

qa.q: How did Shreya's period of seeking lead to her outcome, and how did she live with it around her family?
qa.a: She read verses and commentaries, talked with Ishita the believer and Yusuf the sceptic, and let hard questions stay open, until she settled on keeping her values without a creed. At Diwali she lit lamps beside her grandmother for love, without arguing or pressing anyone.

qa.q: How did Shreya feel about leaving the questions open?
qa.a: She felt calm, without panic, treating the hard questions as worth her time.

qa.q: What could Shreya do if a relative starts to pressure her about belief?
qa.a: She could stay warm and honest, explain that she keeps her values and her family ties, and not argue to win.

grounding: Shows a faith journey's later stages: honest seeking, a personal outcome without belief and with values intact, and living with family in respect and peace.

passage:
Minakshi and Joseph had joined the firm in the same month. Over four years she had sat with him in a hospital waiting room when his father had surgery, and he had brought her soup the week her engagement ended. She could say the shameful thing aloud to Joseph, that she was tired of her manager's tone, and expect only "Same here."

When the senior analyst role opened, Joseph's palms went damp. He dreaded watching everyone else move up without him. That afternoon, in the manager's office, he mentioned, lightly, that Minakshi had complained about the workload and the tone. "Just so you know," he added. He told himself it was business.

A week later Gurpreet, at the coffee machine, said awkwardly, "I assumed you knew that Joseph told the manager what you said." Minakshi's hand froze on the cup. At first she felt nothing, a strange blank, like a room with the furniture removed. Then rage came, hot and fast. Later, in the stairwell, she realised she was grieving twice: for a friend, and for the person she had believed him to be.

qa.q: How did Minakshi learn what Joseph had done?
qa.a: Gurpreet told her at the coffee machine.

qa.q: How does what Joseph did in the manager's office change the meaning of the four years of friendship?
qa.a: Four years of hospital waits and soup made Joseph the person Minakshi could be weakest around. His telling the manager about her complaint, out of dread of being passed over, broke that trust, so she lost both the friend and the person she had believed him to be.

qa.q: What was Minakshi feeling first at the coffee machine?
qa.a: She felt numb, a strange blank, before the rage came.

qa.q: What could Minakshi do next?
qa.a: She could give herself time before reacting, talk with someone she trusts, and later decide calmly whether to speak to Joseph directly.

grounding: Shows a friendship betrayal's early stages: years of loyal support, a colleague's competitive act, and the friend learning the truth from a third person.
